records.source: Παῦλος ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ καὶ Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφὸς τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Κορίνθῳ, σὺν τοῖς ἁγίοις πᾶσιν τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἀχαΐᾳ·
records.gloss: Paul, apostle of Christ Jesus through [the] will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the church of the God the [one] being in Corinth, with the holy [ones] all the [ones] being in whole the Achaia;
pieces: From Paul, an apostle of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus by the will of God, and from Timothy our brother, to the church of God in Corinth, together with all God's holy people throughout Achaia.

L.1: Paul, an apostle of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus through [the] will of God, and Timothy [our] brother, to the church of God that is in Corinth, with all the holy ones who are in the whole of Achaia.

R.1: This letter is from Paul and from our brother Timothy. It was God's will that I, Paul, should be an apostle, sent out by {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus. We are writing to God's church in the city of Corinth, and to all of God's holy people everywhere in the province of Achaia.

decisions.choice: apostle: a messenger sent out with the authority of the one who sends him
alternatives: a missionary or church worker in general
decisions.reason: ἀπόστολος means one who is sent. Paul uses it for those commissioned by the risen Christ to speak for him, and counts himself among them (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:7-9). In this letter his standing as an apostle is itself under attack (chapters 10-13), so the opening words "through the will of God" carry weight: the role was given by God, not claimed by Paul.

decisions.choice: church: the community of believers gathered as God's people
decisions.reason: ἐκκλησίᾳ was the ordinary word for an assembly of citizens. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel gathered before God (Deuteronomy 4:10; 9:10). "Of God" says whose assembly this is, as in 1 Corinthians 1:2. It means the people, not a place of worship.

decisions.choice: Corinth: the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, in southern Greece
decisions.reason: Paul founded the church in Corinth and stayed there a year and a half (Acts 18:1-11). Achaia was the province around it; it held other believers, for example at Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port (Romans 16:1), and at Athens (Acts 17:34). The letter is meant for all of them.

decisions.choice: people set apart as belonging to God
decisions.reason: As in Philippians 1:1, ἁγίοις describes every believer, not a select few: the whole church is God's holy people, as Israel was (Exodus 19:6).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: holy ones (L); God's holy people (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in Philippians 1:1 and Colossians 1:2: in current English "saints" suggests unusually good people, not a whole congregation.

decisions.choice: It was God's will that I, Paul, should be an apostle, sent out by {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus
alternatives: an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God
decisions.reason: As in Colossians 1:1, Readable makes the opening a sentence, says what an apostle is, and adds "city" and "province" so that young readers know what Corinth and Achaia are.

records.heading: Greeting

records.source: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
records.gloss: Grace to you and peace from God Father of us and Lord Jesus Christ.
pieces: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.2: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and [the] Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.2: May God our Father and the Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} show you grace and give you peace.

decisions.choice: one source: God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together
decisions.reason: A single ἀπὸ ("from") governs both names, so Jesus is named with God the Father as the one source of grace and peace, as in Paul's other greetings (Romans 1:7; Philippians 1:2).

decisions.choice: a greeting turned into a blessing
decisions.reason: Greek letters normally opened with a one-word "greetings". Paul replaces it with χάρις (grace), close to it in sound, and adds εἰρήνη (peace), the usual Jewish greeting. It is a wish and a prayer for God's favor and wholeness.

decisions.choice: Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: May ... show you grace and give you peace
decisions.reason: The greeting has no verb. Readable states it as the prayer it is, as Colossians 1:2 does.

records.source: Εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὁ πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν καὶ θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως, ὁ παρακαλῶν ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ θλίψει ἡμῶν, εἰς τὸ δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς παρακαλεῖν τοὺς ἐν πάσῃ θλίψει διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως ἧς παρακαλούμεθα αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Blessed [is] the God and Father of the Lord of us Jesus Christ, the Father of the mercies and God of all comfort, \v 4 the [one] comforting us in all the affliction of us, for the to be able us to comfort the [ones] in every affliction through the comfort with which we are comforted ourselves by the God.
pieces: Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes.
He comforts us in every hardship we face, so that we in turn can comfort people facing any hardship, passing on to them the same comfort God gives us.

L.3: Blessed [is] the God and Father of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
L.4: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those [who are] in any affliction through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

R.3: Let us praise the God and Father of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. He is the Father who shows mercy, and the God who gives every kind of comfort.
R.4: He comforts us in all our troubles. Then we can comfort others when they are in any kind of trouble. We can give them the same comfort God has given us.

decisions.choice: a Jewish blessing of God: praise that declares him worthy
alternatives: a wish that God may be blessed
decisions.reason: Εὐλογητὸς opens the traditional Jewish blessing of God, familiar from the Psalms (Psalm 41:14; 72:18) and used again in Ephesians 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:3. The Greek has no verb; it is a declaration of praise. In most of his letters Paul goes on from the greeting to thank God for his readers (Philippians 1:3; Colossians 1:3); here he blesses God for what God has done for Paul himself.

decisions.choice: God is both the God and the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ
alternatives: God, who is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: One article ὁ covers both θεὸς and πατὴρ, so "of our Lord Jesus Christ" goes with both words. Paul can speak of "the God of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:17), and Jesus speaks of "my Father and your Father, my God and your God" (John 20:17).

decisions.choice: the Father who is merciful and from whom mercy comes
decisions.reason: "Father of mercies" is a Hebrew way of saying "the merciful Father", in which the second noun describes the first. οἰκτιρμῶν is plural, like the Hebrew word for compassion; Jewish prayers called God by much the same title.

decisions.choice: comfort: consolation that also strengthens, giving courage to go on
decisions.reason: The noun παρακλήσεως and the verb παρακαλῶν can mean to urge, to encourage or to comfort. Here they meet suffering, so comfort is meant, but comfort that strengthens, not only soothes. The words come ten times in verses 3-7 and set the theme of the chapter. In the Greek Old Testament the same verb opens Isaiah 40, God's word of comfort to his suffering people.

decisions.choice: affliction: hardship and pressure from outside, including persecution
decisions.reason: θλίψει means pressure that crushes. Paul uses it for the trouble that comes on believers in the world, often from opponents (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 3:3). Verse 8 gives an example from Paul's own life.

decisions.choice: the purpose of God's comfort: to be passed on to others
alternatives: a result Paul happens to notice
decisions.reason: εἰς τὸ with the infinitive states purpose. God comforts Paul so that he can comfort others; the comfort is given to be shared.

decisions.choice: Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: comfort
decisions.reason: One English word for the noun and the verb at every level keeps the repetition that ties verses 3-7 together. "Comfort" is the plainest word for help given in suffering; the meaning decision says it includes strength.

decisions.choice: affliction (L); hardship (B); trouble (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the traditional word. "Affliction" is formal for modern hearers, so Balanced uses "hardship" and Readable "trouble". "Suffering" is kept for a different word in verses 5-7.

decisions.choice: the merciful Father and the God from whom all comfort comes (B); the Father who shows mercy, and the God who gives every kind of comfort (R)
alternatives: the Father of mercies and God of all comfort
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the Hebrew-style phrases (see the meaning decision) instead of copying their form.

decisions.choice: Let us praise
decisions.reason: "Blessed" said of God is church language; Readable says what the blessing does. Literal and Balanced keep "blessed", the form of the Psalms.

records.heading: The God of all comfort

records.source: ὅτι καθὼς περισσεύει τὰ παθήματα τοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς ἡμᾶς, οὕτως διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ περισσεύει καὶ ἡ παράκλησις ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: Because just as abound the sufferings of the Christ to us, so through the Christ abounds also the comfort of us.
pieces: For as the sufferings of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} overflow into our lives, so our comfort also overflows through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.5: For just as the sufferings of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} overflow to us, so also through the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} our comfort overflows.

R.5: We share in the many sufferings of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. In the same way, we receive much comfort through {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: sufferings that come to Christ's people because they belong to him: a share in his own sufferings
alternatives: Christ's sufferings on the cross only
the sorrows expected before the end of the age
decisions.reason: The sufferings "overflow to us", so they are not only Christ's past sufferings but something Paul goes through. Paul speaks of sharing in Christ's sufferings (Philippians 3:10) and of completing them in his own flesh (Colossians 1:24): those united with Christ suffer as he did and because of him.

decisions.choice: to overflow: to be more than enough
decisions.reason: περισσεύει is repeated in both halves of the sentence: the sufferings overflow, and the comfort overflows in equal measure. Paul uses the verb often in this letter (4:15; 8:2; 9:8).

decisions.choice: gives the reason for verse 4: why Paul has comfort to share
decisions.reason: ὅτι ("because, for") ties this verse to the last: Paul can comfort others because, through Christ, the comfort he receives is as great as his sufferings.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article both times, and Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: We share in the many sufferings of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}
alternatives: the sufferings of Christ overflow to us
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "overflow to us" means (see the meaning decision), and uses "many" and "much" for the overflow.

records.source: εἴτε δὲ θλιβόμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως καὶ σωτηρίας· εἴτε παρακαλούμεθα, ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως τῆς ἐνεργουμένης ἐν ὑπομονῇ τῶν αὐτῶν παθημάτων ὧν καὶ ἡμεῖς πάσχομεν, καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡμῶν βεβαία ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν· εἰδότες ὅτι ὡς κοινωνοί ἐστε τῶν παθημάτων, οὕτως καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως.
records.gloss: And whether we are afflicted, for the of you comfort and salvation; whether we are comforted, for the of you comfort, the [one] being at work in endurance of the same sufferings which also we suffer, \v 7 and the hope of us [is] firm for you; knowing that as sharers you are of the sufferings, so also of the comfort.
pieces: If we are afflicted, it is so that you may be comforted and saved. If we are comforted, it is so that you may be comforted too, and that comfort works in you as you patiently endure the same sufferings we also suffer.
So we have a firm hope for you. We know that you are partners in the sufferings, and so you are partners in the comfort too.

L.6: But if we are afflicted, [it is] for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, [it is] for your comfort, which is at work in [your] endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer.
L.7: And our hope for you [is] firm, since we know that as you are sharers in the sufferings, so also [you are sharers] in the comfort.

R.6: If we suffer troubles, it is for your comfort and your salvation. If God comforts us, that is for your comfort too. This comfort gives you strength to keep going patiently when you go through the same sufferings we go through.
R.7: We have a hope for you that cannot be shaken. We know that you share in the sufferings, and in the same way you share in the comfort.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: the order and wording printed here
alternatives: a longer form that adds "and salvation" after the second "your comfort" and moves "and our hope for you is firm" into the middle of verse 6
decisions.reason: Manuscripts arrange the clauses of verses 6-7 in several ways. Many later manuscripts repeat "and salvation" in the second half of verse 6 and place the clause about hope earlier. The SBLGNT follows important early manuscripts in the shorter order. Each form says the same thing: Paul's sufferings and his comfort both serve the Corinthians. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the comfort is at work: it shows its power in them
alternatives: the comfort is produced in them by God
decisions.reason: ἐνεργουμένης can be middle ("is at work, is effective") or passive ("is worked"). Paul uses the middle of this verb for a power at work in people (4:12; Romans 7:5). Either way the comfort is active in the Corinthians as they endure.

decisions.choice: endurance: bearing up steadily under pressure
decisions.reason: ὑπομονῇ is the strength to stay under a load without giving way. It is not a mood but a way of holding on, and here it is the form comfort takes.

decisions.choice: salvation: God's full and final rescue
decisions.reason: σωτηρίας is God's saving work, completed when Christ comes (Philippians 1:28; 2:12). Paul's sufferings serve it because they come with his bringing them the gospel.

decisions.choice: partners: people who have a real share in something together
decisions.reason: κοινωνοί is the word for business partners (Luke 5:10). The Corinthians do not just feel for Paul; they themselves suffer for Christ, and so they truly share in his comfort.

decisions.choice: the ground of Paul's hope: what he knows about sharing
decisions.reason: The participle εἰδότες ("knowing") gives the reason Paul's hope for them is firm: a share in Christ's sufferings brings a share in his comfort.

decisions.choice: the sentence broken into four (B) or six (R)
decisions.reason: Verses 6-7 are one Greek sentence. Balanced and Readable break it where each clause can stand, keeping its order.

decisions.choice: partners
decisions.reason: As in Philippians 1:5-7, "partners" says that the Corinthians have a real share, not just sympathy.

decisions.choice: If God comforts us; a hope for you that cannot be shaken
alternatives: If we are comforted; our hope for you is firm
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who comforts, as verse 4 says, and says what a "firm" hope is.

records.source: Οὐ γὰρ θέλομεν ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοί, ὑπὲρ τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν τῆς γενομένης ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, ὅτι καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἐβαρήθημεν, ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν·
records.gloss: For not we want you to be ignorant, brothers, about the affliction of us the [one] having happened in the Asia, that according to excess beyond power we were weighed down, so that to despair us even of the to live;
pieces: We do not want you to be left unaware, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, of the hardship that came on us in Asia. We were weighed down so heavily, so far past our strength, that we had given up hope even of staying alive.

L.8: For we do not want you to be unaware, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, of our affliction that happened in Asia, that we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond [our] strength, so that we despaired even of living.

R.8: We want you to know, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, about the terrible trouble we had in the province of Asia. The load we had to carry was far too heavy for us. It was so bad that we did not think we would live.

decisions.choice: a formula for introducing important news
alternatives: a complaint that the readers do not know
decisions.reason: Paul uses "we do not want you to be unaware" when he is about to tell his readers something they need to know (Romans 1:13; 1 Corinthians 10:1; 1 Thessalonians 4:13).

decisions.choice: Asia: the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city
decisions.reason: Paul worked in Ephesus for over two years (Acts 19:10). He does not say what the affliction was. Possibilities include the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41), danger he calls fighting wild beasts (1 Corinthians 15:32), imprisonment or severe illness. The Corinthians knew; we do not.

decisions.choice: "we" here is Paul himself, perhaps with his companions
decisions.reason: The letter moves between "I" (1:15-17, 1:23) and "we". Paul often uses "we" of himself and his fellow workers, and sometimes of himself alone. Here the danger is Paul's own, though others may have shared it. The plural does not mean the Corinthians.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί is masculine plural, the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women together.

decisions.choice: to be utterly at a loss, with no way out
decisions.reason: ἐξαπορηθῆναι strengthens a verb meaning to be at a loss. In 4:8 Paul says he is perplexed but not utterly perplexed, using these two verbs; here, in Asia, he was brought to the end of all hope, even of life.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul writes to the whole church, women and men. "Brothers" stays available as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: the province of Asia
decisions.reason: In current English "Asia" means the continent; Readable says that a Roman province is meant.

records.heading: Rescued from death in Asia

records.source: ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὸ ἀπόκριμα τοῦ θανάτου ἐσχήκαμεν, ἵνα μὴ πεποιθότες ὦμεν ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τῷ θεῷ τῷ ἐγείροντι τοὺς νεκρούς·
records.gloss: but ourselves in ourselves the sentence of the death we have had, so that not trusting we may be in ourselves but in the God the [one] raising the dead;
pieces: In fact, we had accepted within ourselves that we were condemned to die. That was so that our confidence would rest, not on ourselves, but on God, who raises the dead.

L.9: But we ourselves had the sentence of death in ourselves, so that we would not be trusting in ourselves but in God who raises the dead.

R.9: Inside ourselves, we felt like people who had been sentenced to death. But that happened so that we would not trust in ourselves. Instead, we would trust in God, who brings dead people back to life.

decisions.choice: a sentence: an official verdict, here a verdict of death
alternatives: an answer from God, given in reply to prayer
decisions.reason: ἀπόκριμα is an official decision, and in inscriptions of the time it can be a ruling given in answer to a request. Paul says he had it "in ourselves": whether or not a court was involved, he had inwardly accepted that he was condemned to die. Some take the word as God's answer to his prayer, which was to trust God; the next clause gives that purpose in any case.

decisions.choice: the perfect tense: the verdict was received and still marks him
decisions.reason: ἐσχήκαμεν is perfect: the experience is past, but its effect remains. Paul writes as one who still lives under its lesson.

decisions.choice: God's purpose in the experience
decisions.reason: ἵνα states purpose: the danger served to turn Paul's trust away from himself to God.

decisions.choice: God who raises the dead: a title of God from Jewish prayer
decisions.reason: A daily Jewish prayer of the time praised God as the one who gives life to the dead, and Paul uses the same kind of title for God in Romans 4:17. Here it is personal: God raised Paul from what he took to be certain death, and he will raise the dead at the end (4:14).

decisions.choice: we had accepted within ourselves that we were condemned to die
alternatives: we had the sentence of death in ourselves
decisions.reason: Balanced says what having the sentence "in ourselves" means: an inner conviction (see the meaning decision).

decisions.choice: who brings dead people back to life
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what raising the dead is.

records.source: ὃς ἐκ τηλικούτου θανάτου ἐρρύσατο ἡμᾶς καὶ ῥύσεται, εἰς ὃν ἠλπίκαμεν ὅτι καὶ ἔτι ῥύσεται, συνυπουργούντων καὶ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τῇ δεήσει, ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: who from so great a death rescued us and will rescue, in whom we have hoped that also still he will rescue, \v 11 helping together also you on behalf of us by the prayer, so that from many faces the to us gift through many may be given thanks for on behalf of us.
pieces: God rescued us from so great a death, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will rescue us. We have fixed our hope on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will rescue us yet again,
as you also work with us by praying for us. Then the gift God has given us through the prayers of many will be met with thanks from many people for our sake.

L.10: who rescued us from so great a death and will rescue [us], on whom we have set our hope that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will yet rescue [us] again,
L.11: as you also help together on our behalf by [your] prayer, so that thanks may be given by many persons on our behalf for the gift [granted] to us through many.

R.10: God rescued us from that terrible danger of death, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will rescue us again. We trust {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to keep on rescuing us,
R.11: and you are helping us by praying for us. Many people are praying. So when God is kind to us and answers their prayers, many people will thank {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done for us.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "so great a death" and "and will rescue"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ here. Some have the present "and rescues", some leave the words out, perhaps because the repeated "will rescue" seemed redundant, and an early papyrus has the plural "deaths". The SBLGNT follows important early manuscripts. The meaning is much the same. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: past, future and continuing rescue: God's rescue in Asia gives a settled hope
decisions.reason: ἐρρύσατο is past, the event in Asia; ῥύσεται looks ahead; ἠλπίκαμεν is perfect, a hope set once and still held, that God "will yet" rescue. The repetition is deliberate: what God did, he will do.

decisions.choice: the Corinthians' prayer goes along with God's rescue
alternatives: a condition: God will rescue only if they pray
decisions.reason: συνυπουργούντων is a participle phrase, "you also helping together". It describes the Corinthians' share in Paul's rescue without making it a strict condition. Paul often asks for prayer as real help (Romans 15:30; Philippians 1:19).

decisions.choice: many persons
alternatives: many faces turned up to God in prayer
decisions.reason: προσώπων means "face" and could also mean "person" in Greek of the time. "From many faces" means from many people. Some see a picture of faces lifted in prayer, but the plain sense is enough.

decisions.choice: a gift of God's grace: here, God's rescue of Paul
alternatives: a spiritual ability given to a believer
decisions.reason: χάρισμα is a gift that comes from God's grace. In 1 Corinthians 12 the word is used for gifts of the Spirit; here the gift is Paul's deliverance.

decisions.choice: "through many" goes with the gift: given in answer to many people's prayers
alternatives: "through many" goes with the thanks: many people giving thanks
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves open which phrase "through many" belongs to. Read with the gift, it says the rescue came through the prayers of many, which verse 11 has just mentioned; "from many persons" already covers the thanks. The general sense is the same either way.

decisions.choice: God rescued us; the gift God has given us
alternatives: who rescued us; the gift to us
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun points back to God in verse 9; Balanced and Readable name him because they begin a new sentence. They also name God as the giver of the gift.

decisions.choice: the purpose clause told as a sequence: many pray, God answers, many give thanks
alternatives: so that thanks may be given by many for the gift given through many
decisions.reason: Readable unfolds the compressed Greek clause into steps a young reader can follow.

records.source: Ἡ γὰρ καύχησις ἡμῶν αὕτη ἐστίν, τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως ἡμῶν, ὅτι ἐν ἁγιότητι καὶ εἰλικρινείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ, οὐκ ἐν σοφίᾳ σαρκικῇ ἀλλ’ ἐν χάριτι θεοῦ, ἀνεστράφημεν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, περισσοτέρως δὲ πρὸς ὑμᾶς·
records.gloss: For the boasting of us this is, the testimony of the conscience of us, that in holiness and sincerity of the God, not in wisdom fleshly but in grace of God, we conducted ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you;
pieces: Here is what we take pride in, and our conscience confirms it: in the world at large, and still more with you, we have behaved with a holiness and sincerity that come from God, guided not by merely human wisdom but by the grace of God.

L.12: For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience: that in holiness and sincerity [that come] from God, not in fleshly wisdom but in [the] grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more toward you.

R.12: There is one thing we are proud of, and our conscience tells us it is true. Wherever we have been in the world, and most of all with you, we have lived in a holy and honest way that comes from God. We did not depend on human cleverness. We depended on the grace of God.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "holiness"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts are divided between two Greek words that differ by only a few letters: ἁγιότητι ("holiness") and a word for simplicity, openness of heart. The second fits Paul's language elsewhere in the letter (11:3) and its use with "sincerity"; the first is rarer and is found in important early manuscripts. The SBLGNT prints "holiness". Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: boasting: a proper pride, a ground for confidence
decisions.reason: καύχησις is a key word of 2 Corinthians. Paul condemns boasting in oneself (10:17; 11:18) but here and in 1:14 uses it of a clear conscience and of the people God has given him. The sense is honest pride in what God has done.

decisions.choice: conscience: inner awareness that judges one's own conduct
decisions.reason: συνειδήσεως is the inner witness that approves or condemns what a person has done (Romans 2:15; 2 Corinthians 4:2). Paul's conscience testifies in his favor.

decisions.choice: holiness and sincerity that God gives
decisions.reason: The genitive "of God" most likely marks the source, matching "by the grace of God" in the next phrase: Paul's integrity is God's work in him.

decisions.choice: merely human wisdom: cleverness that works by the world's standards
decisions.reason: σαρκικῇ ("fleshly") describes what is merely human, without God. Paul sets clever speech and calculation against the power of God in 1 Corinthians 1:17-2:5, and in verse 17 of this chapter he will deny planning "according to the flesh".

decisions.choice: merely human wisdom (B); human cleverness (R)
decisions.reason: "Fleshly" suggests the body to a modern reader; Literal keeps it, while Balanced and Readable give the sense. "Worldly" is avoided because "world" in this verse means the world at large, not something bad.

decisions.choice: take pride in (B); are proud of (R)
decisions.reason: In English "boast" is almost always bad. Balanced and Readable use "pride", which can be good or bad, as the Greek word can; Literal keeps "boasting" to show the link with 10:17 and 11:18.

records.source: οὐ γὰρ ἄλλα γράφομεν ὑμῖν ἀλλ’ ἢ ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε ἢ καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε, ἐλπίζω δὲ ὅτι ἕως τέλους ἐπιγνώσεσθε, καθὼς καὶ ἐπέγνωτε ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ μέρους, ὅτι καύχημα ὑμῶν ἐσμεν καθάπερ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: For not other [things] we write to you but than what you read or also understand, and I hope that until [the] end you will understand, \v 14 just as also you understood us in part, that boast of you we are just as also you of us in the day of the Lord of us Jesus.
pieces: We write you nothing other than what you can read and recognize as true. And I hope you will come to recognize it completely,
as you have already recognized us in part: that we are your reason to be proud, as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.

L.13: For we write nothing else to you than what you read and also understand, and I hope that you will understand fully,
L.14: just as you also did understand us in part, that we are your [reason for] boasting, just as you also [are] ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.

R.13: There is nothing hidden in our letters. We mean exactly what you read and understand. I hope you will understand us completely.
R.14: You understand us partly now. But I hope you will see fully that on the day our Lord Jesus comes back, we will be proud of you, and you will be proud of us.

decisions.choice: no hidden meaning: Paul's letters mean what they plainly say
alternatives: a general remark about clear writing
decisions.reason: Paul plays on two similar verbs, ἀναγινώσκετε ("you read") and ἐπιγινώσκετε ("you recognize, understand"). He is answering a charge that his letters say one thing and he means another (compare 10:9-11). There is nothing "other" behind what the Corinthians read.

decisions.choice: fully: to the point of complete understanding
alternatives: until the end: until the day of the Lord
decisions.reason: ἕως τέλους can mean "completely" or "until the end". Set against "in part" in verse 14, "fully" fits; but the mention of the day of the Lord at the end of verse 14 makes "until the end" possible.

decisions.choice: in part: they understand Paul only partly
decisions.reason: ἀπὸ μέρους can mean "partly" or "some of you". Paul uses it for partial understanding in 1 Corinthians 13:9-12; but the letter also shows that some in Corinth were against him (2:5-6; 10:10), so the other reading is possible.

decisions.choice: a reason for boasting: someone to be proud of
decisions.reason: καύχημα is the ground of boasting, used in a good sense as in Philippians 2:16: on the day of the Lord, Paul and the church will each be the other's reason for pride before Christ.

decisions.choice: the day of Christ's return
decisions.reason: The prophets spoke of "the day of the Lord" (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). Paul applies it to the Lord Jesus, whose coming he awaits (1 Corinthians 1:8; Philippians 1:6).

decisions.choice: recognize
decisions.reason: The verb means both to understand and to acknowledge. Balanced uses "recognize", which has both senses; Literal and Readable use "understand".

decisions.choice: There is nothing hidden in our letters. We mean exactly what you read
alternatives: We write you nothing other than what you read
decisions.reason: Readable states the point Paul is making against the charge of double meaning (see the meaning decision), and names the return of the Lord Jesus as the day meant.

records.source: Καὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πεποιθήσει ἐβουλόμην πρότερον πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλθεῖν, ἵνα δευτέραν χάριν σχῆτε, καὶ δι’ ὑμῶν διελθεῖν εἰς Μακεδονίαν, καὶ πάλιν ἀπὸ Μακεδονίας ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ ὑφ’ ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν.
records.gloss: And in this confidence I was wanting formerly to you to come, so that a second grace you might have, \v 16 and through you to pass through into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you and by you to be sent on into the Judea.
pieces: Confident of this, I had planned to come to you first, to give you a second gift of grace.
I would pass through your city on the way to Macedonia, return to you from Macedonia, and then let you help me on my journey to Judea.

L.15: And with this confidence I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace,
L.16: and to pass through you into Macedonia, and to come again from Macedonia to you, and to be sent on by you to Judea.

R.15: I was sure about this, so I made a plan to visit you first. That way you would receive God's grace twice, through two visits from me.
R.16: I planned to stop with you on my way to Macedonia. Then I would come back to you from Macedonia, and you would help me on my trip to Judea.

decisions.choice: a second gift of God's grace, brought through a second visit
alternatives: a second favor or kindness from Paul
a second chance to show kindness
decisions.reason: χάριν here is not God's grace in the general sense but a particular benefit of it: Paul's visits bring God's gifts (Romans 1:11; 15:29). The plan was to visit Corinth twice, before and after Macedonia, so "second" means a second visit and its blessing.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "grace"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read a similar Greek word meaning "joy", which differs by one letter and fits the mention of joy in verse 24 and 2:3. The SBLGNT follows the reading "grace", found in most early manuscripts. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: first: before going to Macedonia
alternatives: earlier: at an earlier time, before the plan changed
decisions.reason: πρότερον can mean "first" in a sequence or "earlier" in time. Verse 16 sets out the order of the trip: Corinth, Macedonia, Corinth again. Either reading fits the plan that was dropped.

decisions.choice: Paul's changed travel plans
decisions.reason: In 1 Corinthians 16:5-7 Paul planned to go through Macedonia and then come to Corinth. Here he describes a later plan, a double visit. He did not carry it out (1:23; 2:1), and his critics used the change against him. Judea was the goal because he was taking the collection to the believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-4; Romans 15:25-26). Macedonia was the province north of Achaia, with Philippi and Thessalonica.

decisions.choice: to be sent on: helped on a journey with supplies and company
decisions.reason: προπεμφθῆναι was the regular word for a church's help to a traveling preacher: food, money, sometimes companions (Romans 15:24; 1 Corinthians 16:6; Titus 3:13).

decisions.choice: a second gift of grace (B); receive God's grace twice, through two visits from me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the "second grace" was (see the meaning decision) and keep the key word "grace".

decisions.choice: pass through your city (B); stop with you (R)
decisions.reason: "Through you" means through Corinth, where they live.

records.heading: Paul's change of plans

records.source: τοῦτο οὖν βουλόμενος μήτι ἄρα τῇ ἐλαφρίᾳ ἐχρησάμην;
records.gloss: This therefore wanting, [did] I then use the lightness?
pieces: So when I planned this, did I treat it lightly?

L.17: So when I wanted this, did I really act with lightness?

R.17: When I planned all this, I was not careless about it, was I?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
decisions.reason: μήτι introduces a question to which the speaker expects a negative answer. Paul is not unsure; he is rejecting a charge.

decisions.choice: lightness: fickleness, making plans carelessly and dropping them
decisions.reason: ἐλαφρίᾳ means lightness, here in the sense of being unreliable. The article ("the lightness") may point to the very fickleness the Corinthians had accused him of.

decisions.choice: I was not careless about it, was I?
decisions.reason: A tag question shows young readers that the expected answer is "no", as the Greek does.

records.source: ἢ ἃ βουλεύομαι κατὰ σάρκα βουλεύομαι, ἵνα ᾖ παρ’ ἐμοὶ τὸ Ναὶ ναὶ καὶ τὸ Οὒ οὔ;
records.gloss: Or what I plan, according to flesh do I plan, so that there may be with me the Yes yes and the No no?
pieces: Or are my plans made by merely human standards, so that with me it is "Yes, yes" and "No, no" at once?

L.17: Or what I plan, do I plan according to [the] flesh, so that with me there may be "Yes, yes" and "No, no"?

R.17: Do I make plans the way selfish people do? Do I say "Yes, yes" and then "No, no" whenever it suits me?

decisions.choice: by merely human standards: planning for one's own advantage
decisions.reason: κατὰ σάρκα describes plans made the way people do without God, shaped by self-interest. Some in Corinth said Paul lived this way (10:2); he answers the charge here and in verse 12.

decisions.choice: saying yes and no about the same thing: being unreliable
alternatives: an emphatic yes that truly means yes
decisions.reason: Elsewhere a doubled "yes" means a plain, honest yes (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12). Here, with "yes, yes" and "no, no" both "with me", the picture is of a man whose answer can be either, so that no one can rely on his word. Verse 18 confirms this: his word is not "Yes and No".

decisions.choice: by merely human standards (B); the way selfish people do (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 12, Literal keeps "flesh", while Balanced and Readable give the sense.

decisions.choice: at once (B); then ... whenever it suits me (R)
decisions.reason: These words make clear that the doubled yes and no describe unreliability, not emphasis (see the meaning decision).

records.source: πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν ὁ πρὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ ἔστιν Ναὶ καὶ Οὔ.
records.gloss: But faithful [is] the God, that the word of us the [one] to you is not Yes and No.
pieces: But God is faithful, and our word to you is not "Yes" and "No" at once.

L.18: But God [is] faithful, that our word to you is not "Yes and No."

R.18: God is faithful. And just as surely, what we say to you does not mean "Yes" and "No" at the same time.

decisions.choice: a form of oath: as surely as God is faithful
alternatives: a statement with a reason: God is faithful, because our word is not yes and no
decisions.reason: The phrase is like "God is my witness" (verse 23; Romans 1:9). Paul appeals to God's faithfulness to back his own: he is God's messenger, and God is not unreliable.

decisions.choice: our word: what we said to you, including the message we preached
decisions.reason: λόγος can mean speech in general or the message. Paul moves from his plans (verse 17) to his preaching (verse 19): if his message about Christ is reliable, so is his word about lesser things.

decisions.choice: at once (B); at the same time (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 17, the words say that yes and no together mark an unreliable word.

records.source: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ γὰρ υἱὸς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν δι’ ἡμῶν κηρυχθείς, δι’ ἐμοῦ καὶ Σιλουανοῦ καὶ Τιμοθέου, οὐκ ἐγένετο Ναὶ καὶ Οὒ, ἀλλὰ Ναὶ ἐν αὐτῷ γέγονεν·
records.gloss: For the of God Son, Jesus Christ, the [one] among you through us having been preached, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, not did become Yes and No, but Yes in him has become;
pieces: Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, the Son of God, whom Silvanus, Timothy and I proclaimed among you, did not turn out to be "Yes" and "No." In {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} "Yes" has become a reality.

L.19: For the Son of God, Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, who was proclaimed among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, did not become "Yes and No," but in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} it has become "Yes."

R.19: Silvanus, Timothy and I preached to you about Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, the Son of God. He was never "Yes" and "No" at the same time. With {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} it is always "Yes."

decisions.choice: Silvanus: Paul's companion, called Silas in Acts
decisions.reason: Silvanus is the Latin form of the name; Acts calls him Silas. He and Timothy were with Paul when the church in Corinth was founded (Acts 18:5), and they join him in writing 1 and 2 Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:1).

decisions.choice: Christ himself is God's "yes": in him God's word is fully reliable
decisions.reason: Paul's point is not Jesus' speech but who he is: in him God has kept his word, as verse 20 explains. Paul's own reliability rests on the reliability of the Christ he preached.

decisions.choice: past and lasting: Christ did not prove to be yes and no; in him yes has come and remains
decisions.reason: ἐγένετο is aorist, looking at Christ as he was preached; γέγονεν is perfect, a yes that came and still stands.

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: Silvanus, Timothy and I
alternatives: through me and Silvanus and Timothy
decisions.reason: English courtesy puts "I" last; Balanced and Readable also put the preachers first and make them the subject, so the sentence is easier to follow. Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: "Yes" has become a reality (B); it is always "Yes" (R)
alternatives: in him it has become Yes
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the perfect tense, a yes that has come true; Readable says it stands.

records.source: ὅσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι θεοῦ, ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ Ναί· διὸ καὶ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὸ Ἀμὴν τῷ θεῷ πρὸς δόξαν δι’ ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: For as many as promises of God [are], in him [is] the Yes; therefore also through him the Amen to the God for glory through us.
pieces: However many promises God has made, in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} each one is "Yes." So it is through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} too that we answer God with "Amen," and God is given glory through us.

L.20: For as many as [are the] promises of God, in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [is] the "Yes." Therefore also through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [is] the "Amen" to God for glory through us.

R.20: God has made many promises, and in Jesus every one of them is "Yes." That is why we say "Amen" to God through Jesus, and God receives glory through us.

decisions.choice: every promise God has made is kept in Christ
decisions.reason: God's promises in the Old Testament, to Abraham, to David and through the prophets, find their fulfillment in Christ (Romans 15:8; Galatians 3:16). In him God says "yes" to them all.

decisions.choice: Amen: "it is true, let it be so"
decisions.reason: Ἀμὴν is a Hebrew word carried over into Greek untranslated, meaning "firm, true". It answers God's "yes" with the church's agreement.

decisions.choice: the Amen spoken by the church in worship
decisions.reason: Believers said "Amen" aloud in their gatherings to join in prayers and thanksgivings (1 Corinthians 14:16). Paul pictures the congregation saying it to God through Christ.

decisions.choice: "through us": through Paul and his companions, who brought the Corinthians the message and lead their Amen
decisions.reason: The phrase may include the whole church saying Amen, but in the setting of verses 18-19 it points first to the preachers: through their preaching God's yes was heard and the Amen came to be spoken. Either way, God receives the glory.

decisions.choice: in Jesus; through Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, whom "him" refers to (verse 19), because a new paragraph may begin here.

decisions.choice: Amen
decisions.reason: Kept untranslated, as the Greek itself kept it; the word is familiar from prayer.

records.source: ὁ δὲ βεβαιῶν ἡμᾶς σὺν ὑμῖν εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ χρίσας ἡμᾶς θεός, ὁ καὶ σφραγισάμενος ἡμᾶς καὶ δοὺς τὸν ἀρραβῶνα τοῦ πνεύματος ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: And the [one] confirming us with you into Christ and having anointed us [is] God, \v 22 the [one] also having sealed us and having given the down payment of the Spirit in the hearts of us.
pieces: It is God who makes us secure in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, us together with you. God anointed us,
and God sealed us as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own and gave us the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.

L.21: Now the [one] who makes us firm with you in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} and anointed us [is] God,
L.22: who also sealed us and gave [us] the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.

R.21: God is the one who makes both us and you strong in our life with {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. God chose us and gave us a special task.
R.22: God put a mark on us to show that we belong to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. And God put the Spirit in our hearts. The Spirit is like a first payment, a promise that God will give us everything else {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has promised.

decisions.choice: to make firm and secure, as a guarantee makes a contract secure
decisions.reason: βεβαιῶν was used in business for a guarantee that confirms a sale (compare Philippians 1:7). The present participle means God keeps on doing it: he holds both Paul and the Corinthians firm in their union with Christ.

decisions.choice: anointed: set apart by God for his service, as kings, priests and prophets were
alternatives: anointed with oil in a ceremony
decisions.reason: Paul plays on Χριστὸν ("Christ", the Anointed One) and χρίσας ("anointed"). In the Old Testament God anointed kings and prophets for their task (1 Samuel 16:13; Isaiah 61:1). Those joined to the Anointed One share his anointing, which is the gift of the Spirit (compare 1 John 2:20, 27).

decisions.choice: "us" after "with you": all believers, Paul among them
alternatives: Paul and his fellow workers only
decisions.reason: Verse 21 begins with "us with you", so Paul includes the Corinthians. The anointing, sealing and gift of the Spirit could refer to Paul's calling as an apostle, since he is defending his own reliability; but everywhere else Paul speaks of the Spirit as given to every believer (Romans 8:9; Ephesians 1:13).

decisions.choice: sealed: marked as God's own, authentic and protected
decisions.reason: A seal pressed in wax marked a document or goods as belonging to someone and kept them from being tampered with. Paul uses the picture for the Spirit given to believers (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30).

decisions.choice: a down payment: the first installment that guarantees the rest will be paid
alternatives: a pledge returned when the debt is paid
decisions.reason: ἀρραβῶνα is a trade word, borrowed from the Semitic languages, for a deposit that is part of the full price. The Spirit is himself the down payment, the first part of what God will give in full (5:5; Ephesians 1:14).

decisions.choice: God the Father, Christ and the Spirit together in the believer's security
decisions.reason: In two verses Paul names God, Christ and the Spirit, each with a part in making believers secure, as he does again at the end of the letter (13:13).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: down payment
decisions.reason: "Down payment" says that the Spirit is part of what is to come, not just a promise of it; "pledge" can be given back.

decisions.choice: God chose us and gave us a special task; put a mark on us to show that we belong to him; like a first payment, a promise that God will give us everything else
alternatives: anointed us; sealed us; the down payment of the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable explains the three pictures. "Chose us and gave us a special task" is one way of saying what anointing meant; it may say more than Paul does if he means all believers.

records.source: Ἐγὼ δὲ μάρτυρα τὸν θεὸν ἐπικαλοῦμαι ἐπὶ τὴν ἐμὴν ψυχήν, ὅτι φειδόμενος ὑμῶν οὐκέτι ἦλθον εἰς Κόρινθον.
records.gloss: But I [as] witness the God call upon against the my soul, that sparing you no longer I came to Corinth.
pieces: I call on God as witness against my own life if I am not telling the truth: I held back from coming to Corinth again because I wanted to spare you.

L.23: But I call on God [as] witness against my soul that [it was] to spare you [that] I did not come again to Corinth.

R.23: I ask God to be my witness, and to punish me if I am lying. The reason I did not come back to Corinth was that I wanted to spare you pain.

decisions.choice: a solemn oath: may God judge my life if this is false
alternatives: God, who knows my soul, is my witness
decisions.reason: Calling God as witness is an oath. "Against my soul" most naturally means that Paul stakes his life on what he says. The phrase could also mean that God sees into his soul, but either way he swears that he is telling the truth.

decisions.choice: to spare: to hold back from coming with severe discipline
decisions.reason: φειδόμενος means to treat someone gently, holding back from harsh treatment. In 13:2 Paul warns that next time he will not spare them. Another visit at this point would have meant painful confrontation (2:1).

decisions.choice: the visit Paul did not make
decisions.reason: οὐκέτι ("no longer, not again") points to an earlier, painful visit (2:1; 13:2). Instead of returning, Paul wrote a letter "with many tears" (2:3-4). The decision about the visit, not fickleness, is what changed his plan.

decisions.choice: against my own life if I am not telling the truth (B); to punish me if I am lying (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out what the oath formula means (see the meaning decision).

decisions.choice: to spare you pain
decisions.reason: Readable says what Paul spared them, as 2:1-3 goes on to explain.

records.source: οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως, ἀλλὰ συνεργοί ἐσμεν τῆς χαρᾶς ὑμῶν, τῇ γὰρ πίστει ἑστήκατε.
records.gloss: Not that we lord over of you the faith, but co-workers we are of the joy of you, for by the faith you stand.
pieces: We do not mean that we are masters of your faith. Rather, we work alongside you to bring you joy, because you are standing firm in your faith.

L.24: Not that we are masters over your faith, but we are coworkers of your joy, for in the faith you stand.

R.24: We are not your bosses, telling you what to believe. We are working together with you so that you can have joy. And you are standing strong in your faith.

decisions.choice: to rule over as a master
decisions.reason: κυριεύομεν means to be lord or master over something. Paul disclaims any such rule over the Corinthians' faith; the same idea is in 1 Peter 5:3, and in 4:5 Paul calls himself their slave for Jesus' sake.

decisions.choice: a correction of what verse 23 might suggest
decisions.reason: οὐχ ὅτι ("not that") heads off a misunderstanding: talk of sparing them might sound as if Paul controls them. He does not.

decisions.choice: coworkers for your joy: working with you to bring you joy
decisions.reason: συνεργοί is Paul's word for those who work alongside him (Philippians 2:25; Romans 16:3). Here the work aims at their joy, which his visit, had it come then, would have spoiled (2:1-3).

decisions.choice: you stand firm in your faith
alternatives: you stand by means of faith
decisions.reason: The dative πίστει can mean the sphere ("in faith") or the means ("by faith"). Either way, the Corinthians' standing is their own trust in Christ, not Paul's authority over them (compare 1 Corinthians 16:13).

decisions.choice: are masters over (L); are masters of (B)
decisions.reason: "Masters" brings out the link with "lord" and with Paul's language of slaves and masters (4:5).

decisions.choice: We are not your bosses, telling you what to believe
alternatives: we do not rule over your faith
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for someone who gives orders, and says what ruling over faith would mean.
